summary: A landlocked Buddhist kingdom in the eastern Himalayas that became a constitutional monarchy in 2008 and is famous worldwide for its philosophy of 'Gross National Happiness'.

ranking.name: Tibetan Buddhism
ranking.description: Buddhism is said to have been introduced in the 7th century when the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo built the Kyichu Temple in Paro and the Jambay Temple in Bumthang in Bhutan, and in the 8th century Padmasambhava (Guru Rinpoche) came to Bhutan and is regarded as the founder of Bhutanese Buddhism. In 1616 Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal of the Drukpa Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism came from Tibet to Bhutan, unified the regions and established a system uniting religion and government; the Drukpa Kagyu school thereafter became the state religion, and the name of Bhutan in the local language also means 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'.

ranking.name: Hinduism
ranking.description: Hindus are mainly the Lhotshampa (of Nepali descent) of the south, who moved from Nepal to southern Bhutan to clear land in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. In the late 1980s the Bhutanese government pursued a 'One Nation, One People' policy, forcibly imposing the dress and language of the north, and in the early 1990s about 100,000 Lhotshampa were forced to leave Bhutan and lived for many years in refugee camps in Nepal, reducing the proportion of Hindus.

ranking.name: Other (Bon, Christianity, etc.)
ranking.description: Among the other religions, Bon is an ancient faith that was popular on the Tibetan Plateau before Buddhism arrived, and it is still preserved in the folk rituals of some parts of Bhutan. Christians in Bhutan are very few, mainly in the Nepali-descended community of the south; because the government has long restricted proselytizing, the religious activities of Christians are mostly held in private places.

religion.background: Before Buddhism arrived, Bhutan followed Bon and the worship of nature spirits. In the 7th–8th centuries Buddhism arrived with the Tibetan Empire and Padmasambhava, and the legend of Padmasambhava meditating at Tiger's Nest (Paro Taktsang) became an important religious symbol of Bhutan. In 1616 Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal established a government uniting religion and state, with the Drukpa Kagyu school as the state religion, and built dzongs in various places to serve as both monasteries and administrative centers. After the Wangchuck dynasty was founded in 1907, Buddhism remained the core of national identity, and the 2008 constitution established Buddhism as Bhutan's 'spiritual heritage'.

ranking.name: Dzongkha
ranking.description: Dzongkha is a language of western Bhutan belonging to the Tibetic group, close to Tibetan and written in the Tibetan script. 'Dzongkha' means 'the language of the dzong', because it was the language of monks and officials in the dzongs. In 1971 the government formally made it the national language, and from the 1980s the 'One Nation, One People' policy strengthened its promotion, but because Bhutan has more than ten languages, only about a quarter have Dzongkha as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Nepali
ranking.description: Nepali is the language of the Lhotshampa (of Nepali descent) of the south, who began moving to southern Bhutan to clear land from the late 19th century. In the late 1980s the government stopped teaching Nepali in schools and pursued a national-language policy, and in the early 1990s large numbers of Lhotshampa were forced to leave Bhutan, but a considerable share of the population still uses Nepali.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English became the language of instruction in Bhutanese schools from the 1960s, because the Third King, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, was promoting modernization and hired Indian teachers to build a school system across the country. Today English is an important language in education, government documents and diplomacy, but very few have English as their mother tongue.

language.history: Bhutan has about 19 languages, most of them in the Tibeto-Burman family, such as Dzongkha in the west, Tshangla (Sharchopkha) in the east and Bumthangkha in the center. Because of the influence of Tibetan Buddhism, Classical Tibetan (Chöke) was long Bhutan's religious and written language. In 1971 Dzongkha was made the national language, and from the 1960s English became the language of instruction in schools, forming a bilingual education that gives weight to both Dzongkha and English. The 'One Nation, One People' policy of the 1980s strengthened the position of Dzongkha while reducing the room for Nepali in the south.

ranking.name: Ema datshi
ranking.description: Large quantities of green or red chili peppers are the star, stewed together with Bhutanese yak or cow's-milk cheese, extremely spicy and richly cheesy, eaten with red rice.
ranking.history: Ema datshi is regarded as the national dish of Bhutan; 'ema' means chili and 'datshi' means cheese. Chili peppers are native to the Americas and are generally thought to have reached India via the Portuguese in the 16th–17th centuries and then spread to the Himalayan region; in Bhutan they are eaten in large quantities as a vegetable rather than a seasoning. Bhutanese eat chili at almost every meal, and rooftops covered with drying red chilies are a common sight in autumn.

ranking.name: Bhutanese red rice
ranking.description: A red short-grain rice unique to Bhutan, pink when cooked, with a slightly sticky texture and a nutty aroma, the staple of every Bhutanese meal.
ranking.history: Bhutanese red rice is grown mainly in areas above about 2,000 meters in elevation, such as the Paro Valley, irrigated with glacial meltwater from the Himalayas, and is one of the few rice varieties in the world able to grow at high altitude. Rice has sacred significance in Bhutanese culture and is traditionally used in religious offerings. In recent years red rice has also been exported to countries such as the United States and has become a representative agricultural product of Bhutan.

ranking.name: Bhutanese momo
ranking.description: Half-moon or round dumplings with a flour wrapper filled with yak meat, pork, cheese or cabbage and steamed, often eaten with chili sauce.
ranking.history: Momo originated in Tibet and is generally thought to have reached the Himalayan regions of Bhutan, Nepal and northern India with Tibetan Buddhism and merchants; the name is related to the Chinese word for steamed bun ('mo mo'). In Bhutan, momo is a common snack at festivals, markets and family gatherings, and versions with Bhutanese cheese have also developed. It is one of the most popular foods eaten out in Bhutan.

ranking.name: Thukpa (noodle soup)
ranking.description: A hot noodle soup cooked with noodles, sliced meat and vegetables, with a broth made from bones or meat and seasoned with chili, suited to cold weather.
ranking.history: Thukpa originated in eastern Tibet, and its name means 'noodle soup' in Tibetan; it spread with Tibetan merchants and migrants to the Himalayan regions of Bhutan, Nepal and India. In high-altitude Bhutan with its cold winters, hot noodle soup is a warming home-cooked food. It also reflects the long-standing religious and trade ties between Bhutan and Tibet.

ranking.name: Butter tea
ranking.description: Tea leaves are boiled into a strong tea, then butter and salt are added and blended by churning in a wooden tea churn, giving a rich, salty, savory flavor that provides calories and warmth.
ranking.history: Butter tea is a traditional drink of the Himalayan plateau, originating in Tibet, where tea leaves were first transported from China along the Tea Horse Road. In cold high-altitude regions, tea with butter added replenishes calories and prevents chapped lips. In Bhutan, butter tea is the basic courtesy offered to guests and is also offered at monastery rituals and Buddhist festivals, usually enjoyed with puffed rice or dry rice.
